steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a medical imaging paper that presents a new one-stage detector for small lesions. Motivate why small lesions matter and why they are hard to detect, review how lesion detection has evolved up to CNNs and where patch-based and anchor-based methods fall short, introduce our approach and the two test cases, and close with the paper's structure.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Detecting small lesions in medical images has become an interesting area of research. It is very relevant in medicine, especially in fields like Radiology and Oncology, where a timely diagnosis of the disease is essential. Small lesions are mainly characterized by their limited size, and they can be very different in nature depending on where they are and which tissue is involved. In many real-world scenarios, identifying and classifying small lesions is a challenging and critical diagnostic process. For example, retinal microaneurysms are the earliest sign of diabetic retinopathy, and they are caused by small local expansion of capillaries in the retina. In ischemic stroke imaging, identifying a small occlusion early is crucial in order to start treatment in time. In cancer diagnosis, many forms of cancer start as small lesions before they grow and spread, for example breast calcifications, which are one of the most important diagnostic markers of breast lesions, or pulmonary nodules, which can be the first stage of a primary lung cancer. Being able to detect small lesions early and accurately can make a difference in the treatment and prognosis of patients and can have a big impact on patient health. Interpreting medical images manually can take a lot of time and it is susceptible to human error, especially when the task is localizing and identifying small lesions in the full image space.

Research on automatic lesion detection methods has a long tradition. Traditional image processing methods like thresholding, edge detection and morphological operations can be effective for detecting small lesions in images where the structures are clear and well defined. But these methods are limited when there is noise and variability in the medical images. Machine Learning, and Deep Learning in particular, helps to improve the reliability, performance and accuracy of diagnosing systems for specific diseases. In fact, the first lesion detection system based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) was already proposed in 1995, to detect lung nodules in X-ray images. But CNNs became really popular only in the last ten years, thanks to their remarkable performance in computer vision, and they quickly became the preferred solution for automated medical lesion detection. The reason for this success is that they can learn hierarchical representations directly from the images, instead of using handcrafted features based on domain-specific knowledge. CNNs build features with increasing relevance, from texture up to higher order features like local and global shape.

  - patch problems esp. small lesions (cite): need local appearance + global context about location; not possible in patch architectures (cite), even multi-scale -> lesion can be missed
  - alternative: anchoring object detection from computer vision (cite), e.g. RetinaNet (cite), adaptable to lesion detection (cite)
  - difficulties with very small objects: (i) extremely small vs natural objects; (ii) lesions and non-lesions look similar (cite)
- Our proposal
  - one-stage end-to-end detector, new anchoring technique for small lesions in medical images
  - classical anchors: anchor boxes for scale/aspect ratio of object classes; ours pixel-based, moves towards lesion

  - effective for small lesions in whole image space
  - evaluation: microcalcifications on digital mammograms, microaneurysms on digital fundus images

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Detecting small lesions in medical images has become an interesting area of research. It is very relevant in medicine, especially in fields like Radiology and Oncology, where a timely diagnosis of the disease is essential. Small lesions are mainly characterized by their limited size, and they can be very different in nature depending on where they are and which tissue is involved. In many real-world scenarios, identifying and classifying small lesions is a challenging and critical diagnostic process. For example, retinal microaneurysms are the earliest sign of diabetic retinopathy, and they are caused by small local expansion of capillaries in the retina. In ischemic stroke imaging, identifying a small occlusion early is crucial in order to start treatment in time. In cancer diagnosis, many forms of cancer start as small lesions before they grow and spread, for example breast calcifications, which are one of the most important diagnostic markers of breast lesions, or pulmonary nodules, which can be the first stage of a primary lung cancer. Being able to detect small lesions early and accurately can make a difference in the treatment and prognosis of patients and can have a big impact on patient health. Interpreting medical images manually can take a lot of time and it is susceptible to human error, especially when the task is localizing and identifying small lesions in the full image space.

Research on automatic lesion detection methods has a long tradition. Traditional image processing methods like thresholding, edge detection and morphological operations can be effective for detecting small lesions in images where the structures are clear and well defined. But these methods are limited when there is noise and variability in the medical images. Machine Learning, and Deep Learning in particular, helps to improve the reliability, performance and accuracy of diagnosing systems for specific diseases. In fact, the first lesion detection system based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) was already proposed in 1995, to detect lung nodules in X-ray images. But CNNs became really popular only in the last ten years, thanks to their remarkable performance in computer vision, and they quickly became the preferred solution for automated medical lesion detection. The reason for this success is that they can learn hierarchical representations directly from the images, instead of using handcrafted features based on domain-specific knowledge. CNNs build features with increasing relevance, from texture up to higher order features like local and global shape.

A typical CNN architecture for medical image analysis is applied to subparts of an image that contain candidate lesions or background. This means that the image is divided into patches of equal size that partially overlap, and each patch is processed by itself. Then the output image is formed by putting the processed patches back together. Patch-based methods are widely used, but they have several problems, especially for small lesion detection, where an accurate detection needs both local information about how the lesion looks and global contextual information about where it is. This combination is typically not possible in patch-based learning architectures, and even with a multi-scale approach the appearance of a small lesion can be missed. Another option is to use the anchoring object detection methods of computer vision, like RetinaNet, which can be adapted for lesion detection problems. These methods have difficulties when the objects to detect are very small, mainly for two reasons: (i) lesions are extremely small compared to natural objects; (ii) lesions and non-lesions look similar, so it is difficult to detect them effectively.

We propose a new one-stage end-to-end detector based on a new kind of anchoring technique that is customised for small lesion detection in medical images. Classical anchor methods use anchor boxes to capture the scale and aspect ratio of specific classes of objects, while the anchor we propose is pixel-based and it moves towards the lesion to be detected. We called this new architecture GravityNet and the new anchors gravity points, because they are distributed over the whole image and they seem to be “attracted” by hypothetical “gravitational masses” located in the centres of the lesions. This gravitational anchoring turns out to be particularly effective when small lesions have to be detected in the whole image space. To evaluate the performance of our approach we focused on two small lesions: microcalcifications on digital mammograms and microaneurysms on digital fundus images. In both cases the lesions take up only few pixels in the image, so there are limited features to distinguish them from the surrounding tissues. So localizing them accurately is a main challenge, because of how they look and because their contextual backgrounds are heterogeneous.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives a brief overview of object detection techniques in medical images and so of small lesion detection methods. Section 3 introduces the proposed method. Section 4 reports the experimental analysis, and the results follow in Section 5. Finally, Sections 6 and 7 end the paper with discussion and conclusions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Detection of small lesions in medical images has emerged as a compelling area of research, which holds significant relevance in medicine, especially in fields like Radiology and Oncology, where a timely disease diagnosis is essential [1]. Small lesions are primarily characterized by a limited size and can vary greatly in nature depending on their location and the involved tissue. In numerous real-world scenarios, the identification and classification of small lesions is a challenging and critical diagnostic process. For example, retinal microaneurysms are the earliest sign of diabetic retinopathy and are caused by small local expansion of capillaries in the retina [2]. In ischemic stroke imaging, early identification of small occlusions is crucial to initiate timely treatment [3]. In cancer diagnosis, many forms of cancer originate as small lesions before they grow and spread, such as breast calcifications, which are one of the most important diagnostic markers of breast lesions [4], or pulmonary nodules, which can be the first stage of a primary lung cancer [5]. The ability to detect small lesions early and accurately can make a difference in the treatment and prognosis of patients and have a substantial impact on patient health. Manual interpretation of medical images can be time-consuming and susceptible to human error, especially when the task involves localizing and identifying small lesions within the full image space [6].

There is a long tradition of research on automatic lesion detection methods [7]. Traditional image processing methods, such as thresholding, edge detection, and morphological operations, can be effective for detecting small lesions in images with clear and well-defined structures. However, these methods are limited by the presence of noise and variability in medical images. Machine Learning, and in particular Deep Learning, helps to enhance the reliability, performance, and accuracy of diagnosing systems for specific diseases [8]. In fact, the first lesion detection system based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) was proposed back in 1995 to detect lung nodules in X-ray images [9]. However, only in the last ten years have CNNs acquired great popularity, thanks to their remarkable performance in computer vision [10], rapidly becoming the preferred solution for automated medical lesion detection [11,12,13,14]. This success is due to their ability to learn hierarchical representations directly from the images, instead of using handcrafted features based on domain-specific knowledge. CNNs are able to build features of increasing relevance, from texture to higher order features like local and global shape [15].

A typical CNN architecture for medical image analysis is applied to subparts of an image containing candidate lesions or background: the image is divided into partially overlapping patches of equal size, and each patch is processed individually. The output image is then formed by reassembling the processed patches [16]. Although patch-based methods are widely used, they suffer from several problems, especially in the case of small lesion detection [17], where accurate detection requires both local information about the appearance of the lesion and global contextual information about its location. This combination is typically not possible in patch-based learning architectures [18], even with a multi-scale approach, where the appearance of a small lesion can be missed. An alternative is to use the anchoring object detection methods of computer vision [19], like RetinaNet [20], which can be adapted to lesion detection problems [21]. These methods face difficulties when the objects to be detected are very small, mainly for two reasons: (i) lesions have an extremely small size compared to natural objects; (ii) lesions and non-lesions have similar appearances, which makes it difficult to detect them effectively [22].

We propose a novel one-stage end-to-end detector based on a new type of anchoring technique customised to small lesion detection in medical images. Unlike classical anchor methods, which use anchor boxes to capture the scale and aspect ratio of specific classes of objects, the proposed anchor is pixel-based and moves towards the lesion to be detected. We named this new architecture GravityNet and the new anchors gravity points, because they are distributed over the whole image and seem to be “attracted” by hypothetical “gravitational masses” located in the centres of the lesions. This gravitational anchoring proves to be particularly effective when small lesions have to be detected in the whole image space. To evaluate the performance of the proposed approach, we focused on two small lesions: microcalcifications on digital mammograms and microaneurysms on digital fundus images. In both cases, the lesions occupy only a few pixels within an image, leaving limited features to distinguish them from the surrounding tissues. Their accurate localization therefore becomes a main challenge, due to their appearance and to the heterogeneity of their contextual backgrounds.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives a brief overview of object detection techniques in medical images and of small lesion detection methods. Section 3 introduces the proposed method. Section 4 reports the experimental analysis, followed by the results in Section 5. Finally, Sections 6 and 7 close the paper with discussion and conclusions.
